The evident success of the Israeli and U.S. strikes on Iran presents a heretofore unimaginable opportunity to break out of — or at least greatly mitigate — this dilemma.

In the wake of the recent strikes, Iran’s capacity to draw the United States into a prolonged and draining conflict has been severely curtailed. It has lost the bulk of its air defenses, most of its drones and best fighter planes, perhaps as much as half of its ballistic missiles and all or a large part of its nuclear infrastructure. Its leadership cadres have been thinned out and the regime itself is greatly weakened. It will take quite some time for Iran to recover its ability to threaten the existing order in the Middle East.

Israel achieved its success by pursuing an approach known as strategic sequencing. Faced with an encircling array of enemies too powerful to defeat in unison, it employed a combination of bold strikes and creative diplomacy to neutralize them in turn, starting with the smaller ones and working its way up to the top threat. Doing so ensured that, when the main contest came, Israel would be able to concentrate its forces on the decisive spot while Iran would be deprived of the diversionary benefits of its friends and proxies.

Iran’s prostration paves the way for the United States to pursue a similar strategy on a global scale. Except instead of relying on force backed by diplomacy, the U.S. approach should be the reverse: creative diplomacy, backed by the threat of overwhelming military power. Against Iran, for example, the Trump administration adhered to a “diplomacy first” approach, resorting to force only when that option had run its course.

Applying this sequencing logic requires the U.S. to avoid getting sucked into a deeper set of objectives in the Middle East. The worst thing the U.S. could do now would be to embark on a policy of regime change in Iran, as some are advocating. Instead, it should adhere to the narrow goal of removing Iran’s nuclear capabilities. And it should resist calls to beef up permanent U.S. forces in the region and, as soon as possible, initiate a drawdown.

Sticking to “diplomacy first” is not a call for passivity. To the contrary, it will require persistence and attention. Several regional victories are within reach, including brokering a Turkish-Israeli understanding over Syria that prevents it from becoming the flash point for another conflict; completing the process of Israeli-Saudi normalization begun in the first Trump administration; and working with Sunni Arab states to close off avenues for the reemergence of the Islamic State.
The overarching goal should be a regional balance of power that relies primarily on local forces to maintain stability.

With Iran licking its wounds, the administration would be in a strong position to turn its attention to its next-biggest problem: Russia. As with Iran, President Donald Trump has laid a predicate for diplomacy with Vladimir Putin. And like Iran, Putin has so far scorned the opening. But Iran’s setbacks might improve the conditions for a diplomatic breakthrough. For the foreseeable future, Iran will be reorienting military munitions bound for Russia to meet its own desperate needs at home. Trump’s recent success in bucking up NATO defense spending and his nod toward potentially renewing military support for Ukraine could provide further impetus for Putin to agree to serious talks. Even a temporary ceasefire would be a boon, as it would buy more time to pick up the pace of European rearmament, which is key to deterring future Russian adventurism.

In both the Middle East and Europe, the goal is not to solve these crises but to park them long enough to allow the United States and its allies to regain control of the clock. Indeed, the whole point of sequencing is to limit the likelihood that the U.S. military will be called upon to conduct big interventions of the sort that cost us so much blood and treasure in the past.
